title: SQL Fundamentals: Selecting, Filtering, and Joining

questions.question: You want to keep only the groups whose COUNT(*) is at least 2, after aggregation. Which clause do you use?
questions.rationale: HAVING filters groups after GROUP BY and aggregates are computed, while WHERE filters individual rows before grouping — aggregates are not even allowed in WHERE.

questions.question: Which predicate correctly finds students whose city is missing?
questions.rationale: Any comparison with NULL yields unknown, not true, so city = NULL never matches; SQL provides IS NULL as the only correct test for a missing value.

questions.question: On the sample course table (Databases, Networks, AI, Compilers), what does SELECT title FROM course WHERE title LIKE '%s' return?
questions.rationale: The % wildcard matches any run of characters, so '%s' keeps titles ending in s — Databases and Networks.

questions.question: Five students live in three different cities. How many rows does SELECT DISTINCT city FROM student return?
questions.rationale: DISTINCT collapses duplicate output rows, so the three distinct city values — one row each — are returned, answering which cities exist rather than who lives there.

questions.question: On the sample data (5 students, 5 enrolments, Eshan enrolled in nothing), how many rows does SELECT ... FROM student s LEFT JOIN enrolment e ON s.student_id = e.student_id return?
questions.rationale: The inner-join pairs are 5, and the LEFT JOIN adds Eshan's row with NULLs in every enrolment column because his row is kept even without a match.

questions.question: What is the difference between COUNT(*) and COUNT(city)?
options: COUNT(*) counts rows; COUNT(city) skips rows where city is NULL
COUNT(city) is faster in every case
questions.rationale: COUNT(*) counts every row of the group, while COUNT(column) counts only rows where that column is not NULL — a distinction that matters whenever the column can be missing.

questions.question: In a SELECT with WHERE, GROUP BY, and HAVING, which clause is evaluated first?
questions.rationale: Logical evaluation runs FROM first to assemble the row source, then WHERE, GROUP BY, HAVING, and only then SELECT projects the output columns.

questions.question: On the sample data (5 students, 5 enrolments, all enrolments match a student), how many rows does an INNER JOIN of student and enrolment on student_id return?
questions.rationale: An INNER JOIN keeps only matched pairs; all five enrolment rows match a student, so the result has exactly 5 rows — one per enrolment.

questions.question: Which query lists students enrolled in course C1 using a subquery?
options: SELECT name FROM student WHERE student_id IN (SELECT student_id FROM enrolment WHERE course_id = 'C1')
SELECT name FROM student WHERE course_id = 'C1'
SELECT name FROM enrolment WHERE student_id IN student
SELECT name FROM student GROUP BY course_id = 'C1'
questions.rationale: The IN subquery first collects the student_ids from enrolment where course_id is C1, then the outer query keeps matching students — Aisha, Boris, and Chen on the sample data.

questions.question: A developer joins a 5-row and a 4-row table but forgets the ON clause. How many rows come back?
questions.rationale: Without an ON condition the inner join degenerates into a CROSS JOIN, pairing every row with every row: 5 times 4 is 20 — the tell-tale sign of a missing join predicate.
